$P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186404120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404120} :answer-field/id #uuid "5324a7ce-971d-53cb-b107-19a127a08e1f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404115}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f53e1d4c-a53d-5c3e-8ae8-0e080a8e331f" :question/math-academy-id "q-80496" :question/problem "Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c086434a-2e61-5437-a45d-1dd3277fb4b0"} {:db/id 17592186436964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348376 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b5beb30-0a75-5fc1-9136-9135683b1b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346129} {:answer/id #uuid "70a5b71d-efb0-58ab-af42-12eed66f2bb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346339} {:answer/id #uuid "783aadac-abc2-5341-8883-bae757b2fee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -11\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346406} {:answer/id #uuid "78aeeb6e-6d38-58dc-93e3-4da1e56572c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346408} {:answer/id #uuid "df14a525-a2b3-5a1d-8fb5-695c415e41e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186347312}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347312} :answer-field/id #uuid "feb4a3c4-e3c2-59e1-b4f8-a58de2ef0e9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e9500f77-53af-537c-9030-31932253fda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-80372" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and

find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "260bb0c0-f4cc-5171-8f8e-251abb929092" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436963}} {:db/id 17592186436963 :step/content {:db/id 17592186404114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20692b0c-ecf3-5857-b371-5e00dd088456" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c086434a-2e61-5437-a45d-1dd3277fb4b0"} {:db/id 17592186436964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348376 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b5beb30-0a75-5fc1-9136-9135683b1b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346129} {:answer/id #uuid "70a5b71d-efb0-58ab-af42-12eed66f2bb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346339} {:answer/id #uuid "783aadac-abc2-5341-8883-bae757b2fee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -11\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346406} {:answer/id #uuid "78aeeb6e-6d38-58dc-93e3-4da1e56572c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346408} {:answer/id #uuid "df14a525-a2b3-5a1d-8fb5-695c415e41e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186347312}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347312} :answer-field/id #uuid "feb4a3c4-e3c2-59e1-b4f8-a58de2ef0e9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e9500f77-53af-537c-9030-31932253fda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-80372" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and

Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix." :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$

\frac{5 \cdot 4}{4 \cdot 4} &= \frac{20}{16}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}5}}{{\color{red}10}}

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,-5)}=-2{e}^{2(0)}=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278288 :question/id #uuid "2b1f8f7b-fd82-5c84-a276-7fa2fd9b071a" :question/math-academy-id "q-160383" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27184dd5-9306-5151-ba71-71c0184555b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186275833} {:answer/id #uuid "921684d8-1a85-53da-b8a7-23bd356d4d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186276799} {:answer/id #uuid "a6b6ecd9-7efa-5fbf-99f4-87cf3cf2fc2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186276980} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f4d180-9148-56f8-af89-c87393729376" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186277007} {:answer/id #uuid "bc4ef6cf-c02f-531a-934f-84c5afac9290" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276799} :answer-field/id #uuid "3f823688-c59b-5a64-9e51-9b7c368087e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277821}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ \frac{v}{u}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278291 :question/id #uuid "2443aa6d-e746-5170-93b3-e30684a9a33b" :question/math-academy-id "q-160402"} {:db/id 17592186278296 :question/id #uuid "861c1236-2662-5b7d-b150-03b6774d0f17" :question/math-academy-id "q-160427"} {:db/id 17592186278297 :question/id #uuid "19415143-780a-5182-8164-c1af6838225c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160428"} {:db/id 17592186278298 :question/id #uuid "876a5d15-9cbd-5150-8246-c71dbabaa45c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160431" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09e0e11f-ca64-573d-aa4a-39c0085748ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186275562} {:answer/id #uuid "2571ec42-1410-5512-abb4-5d9f33e67cf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186275817} {:answer/id #uuid "6056f233-baaf-59fc-ab26-47501271c259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186276339} {:answer/id #uuid "e97346e5-01ac-55ce-b840-edd902ee3c65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277517} {:answer/id #uuid "fa81b135-dfdc-52eb-85bc-1dd61c22d3d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186277669}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186277517} :answer-field/id #uuid "946d36e5-48fa-5671-b5c2-6b9df0953fbc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277988}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{v}^{2}+uv \\ v-u\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383515 :question/id #uuid "b7031c6b-f8db-5a21-9b28-fac40f0a2c66" :question/math-academy-id "q-160434"} {:db/id 17592186417356 :question/id #uuid "2756cd36-f06f-563c-8e51-e0b858d03f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-160387" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e0d4b0b-8093-5290-b6b4-484e2a3c019b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186417350} {:answer/id #uuid "3f52c558-a8f4-5f12-84e4-136a7b9663ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186417351} {:answer/id #uuid "ad3faf64-35fa-5814-9c5b-2c546aef7f2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186417352} {:answer/id #uuid "c802b759-c3a3-5234-a525-52e3dcf0d733" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "22" :db/id 17592186417353} {:answer/id #uuid "df929076-a9d7-5c37-b534-2a48f5c0f2ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186417354}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186417353} :answer-field/id #uuid "b6520f4c-cce8-5e56-adce-0289e4c3517a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186417355}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3{u}^{2}+2v$ and $y(u,v)=u+2{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =6u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =4v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}6u & 2 \\ 1 & 4v\end{aligned}| \\  & =6u\cdot 4v-2\cdot 1 \\  & =24uv-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=24(1)(1)-2=22.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129282 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128860 :question/id #uuid "32f92fce-b4b9-5e7a-9fe0-255b15edf312" :question/math-academy-id "e-12417"} :knowledge-point/id $$

$$

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}

"Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 4 & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv+4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4uv+4 & >0 \\ -4uv & >-4 \\ uv & <1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives the solution $v<\frac{1}{u}$ for $u>0$ and $v>\frac{1}{u}$ for $u<0.$

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=\frac{1}{u}
$$

defines a hyperbola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

:question/problem "Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (2v)-(2u)\cdot 1 \\  & =2v-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2v-2u & <0 \\ 2v & <2u \\ v & <u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](images/11/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](images/0d/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](images/09/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](images/23/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :tutorial/id #uuid "c831da3f-8fff-5c5b-8be5-f3602a7303ba" {:db/id 17592186130226}} {:db/id 17592186130225 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "eadcf9f2-f662-5ba3-8bbc-b9166dfa1142" :step/math-academy-id 44550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130065}} {:db/id 17592186130226 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation 

$$
\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)

- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where
![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) 

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$
J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}
$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/content "We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](images/11/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](images/0d/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](images/09/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](images/23/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :tutorial/id #uuid "c831da3f-8fff-5c5b-8be5-f3602a7303ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4147 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5564d0a2-de60-5f46-b603-c6061aab85f2" :step/math-academy-id 25202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130225}} {:db/id 17592186130392 :tutorial/content "We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](images/0d/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](images/09/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](images/23/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :tutorial/id #uuid "c831da3f-8fff-5c5b-8be5-f3602a7303ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4147 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130225 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} :step/id {:db/id 17592186130226 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation 

$$
\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)

- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where
![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) 

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$
J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}
$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7673 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "0e6a94d3-c32f-5582-98ea-69a8605ef653" :step/math-academy-id 44558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130230}} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a571cf4-d621-5149-95d3-896e62b990d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-161875" :question/problem "Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(0,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u-{v}^{2} \\ u+v\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2v) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,3)} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v)\,{|}_{u=0\,v=3} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(3) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|6|\cdot \delta A \\  & =6\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68b725b2-e4f6-5584-8b86-cedb8363d41b"} {:db/id 17592186406805 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129509 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e468aabf-e6e4-5599-81b1-17dc6d355954" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/13/1368ee41963c1abcc320d2cd35449c08599582f37c7d68f750e137fcdcd2e57b.png" :db/id 17592186389030} {:answer/id #uuid "bdeedbec-6bdf-59e7-9b2b-b9d5e4e3ee50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/d4/d477a9f312fc2fb0a5a4c2d13164c96118aa70b53cf23db80be9ec698151e6fd.png" :db/id 17592186389031} {:answer/id #uuid "a24ff250-c577-5a6e-8589-b7fa78f56034" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/fe/fe7bb422a3f992ea88a900e63b2c55df99bce3a785929901c248abadfadf23f1.png" :db/id 17592186389032} {:answer/id #uuid "ddf74745-74d7-5023-8d2f-494bd3a4b62a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/15/154f70201a5a00737d8df61952f5600ff91a2373df07b0b54680fe84e048402c.png" :db/id 17592186389033} {:answer/id #uuid "c8a52325-f624-5716-886a-b507033c0141" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/09/090bab0ac1c6356010d83a6ad54c59b53b7dd12062fb5e331a936ce3f3a1b411.png" :db/id 17592186389034}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389032} :answer-field/id #uuid "391991ce-c7bf-55cb-8662-29196fd230b1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389029}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4471fd6f-9a7d-5e2e-b974-bcbd5ed1ceb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-160601" :question/problem "Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 4 & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv+4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4uv+4 & >0 \\ -4uv & >-4 \\ uv & <1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

defines a hyperbola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.

$$

T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fba89b3b-6b30-58fc-958c-99b3a9d49bb0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406805}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186417359} :activity/id #uuid "5eeaa0e4-09d3-5d55-9a9f-ba1c84383049" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048219 :topic/id #uuid "893b600f-8843-5755-aed4-951036b65cbd" :topic/math-academy-id 1999} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186417357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278298 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09e0e11f-ca64-573d-aa4a-39c0085748ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186275562} {:answer/id #uuid "2571ec42-1410-5512-abb4-5d9f33e67cf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186275817} {:answer/id #uuid "6056f233-baaf-59fc-ab26-47501271c259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186276339} {:answer/id #uuid "e97346e5-01ac-55ce-b840-edd902ee3c65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277517} {:answer/id #uuid "fa81b135-dfdc-52eb-85bc-1dd61c22d3d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186277669}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186277517} :answer-field/id #uuid "946d36e5-48fa-5671-b5c2-6b9df0953fbc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277988}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "876a5d15-9cbd-5150-8246-c71dbabaa45c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160431" :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{v}^{2}+uv \\ v-u\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "51873d91-9d02-596a-8782-ed5264ede6c4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417358}} {:db/id 17592186417358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281352 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48838786-15c4-529e-9b61-9a4ae3631e27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/30/3033f0ae73e3f484fc5d3d65e388062feba1824fb3da9971d560cf2f518f49bb.png" :db/id 17592186279238} {:answer/id #uuid "644450bf-23df-5be6-9017-bc23e84a13fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/83/8382e54c1f91ff0e07910c1250c046413814748d9e7ef8968984b7223b43afcc.png" :db/id 17592186279504} {:answer/id #uuid "71de0d63-b9fe-5bf9-98a3-3aa0f0728bad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/fe/fe7bb422a3f992ea88a900e63b2c55df99bce3a785929901c248abadfadf23f1.png" :db/id 17592186279627} {:answer/id #uuid "743bb53f-15e9-5c76-9499-48070c482fc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/7f/7f214af0b5d71689ec7f21fff043e1779f1d3244c13fdbaf7b8df7f408d66298.png" :db/id 17592186279641} {:answer/id #uuid "9e8384cd-3f08-52be-b19d-6807ce1004b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/14/14015cadab7d5dc8a9c33d0c1a57a44a79506bd01ba9b1cfe8ec1d280eb3fbb6.png" :db/id 17592186279998}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279504} :answer-field/id #uuid "158dba50-6c99-530b-a3b4-71c1f3ef60c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280870}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "613ff480-77bb-508e-adea-361b7545c613" :question/math-academy-id "q-161838" :question/problem "Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (2v)-(2u)\cdot 1 \\  & =2v-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2v-2u & <0 \\ 2v & <2u \\ v & <u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality.

:question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
y'-6y = f(x), \qquad y(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution $y_p$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution $y_p$ satisfies $y_p(1)=0.$*

![](images/d9/d95dc53c303ddf919518e2270cfe6f4314712b414a65f54fb7d228783fa0e214.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form $y' + P(x)y = f(x)$ is given by

$$
y = y_c + y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of $y' - 6y = 0$ is

$$
y_c = Ae^{6x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator $y' - 6y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x) \sim Ae^{6x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=4.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =A{e}^{6(1)}+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 4 & =A{e}^{6}+0 \\ A & =4{e}^{-6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
y_c = (4e^{-6})e^{6x} = 4e^{6x-6}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x) \sim 
\bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{4e^{6x-6}} +
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049288} {:db/id 17592186231565 :question/id #uuid "5c1a49a3-d524-53b2-a5dc-a7db56f9b9c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343430" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231418 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "742531ae-be2d-5fc8-8ef8-4f745c93bacd" :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "6f6ad64c-d62f-565f-ba15-8bbc501a2f16" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186230282}] :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

y''+ 7\pi^2 y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=0, \quad y'(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

![](images/9f/9f77e2dc9619cf5cb270cd68efaf2432a8dbf738e06b33dcdcc18602b5032b1b.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form $y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)$ is given by $y = y_c + y_p,$ where $y_c$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution $y_p.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
y_p(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation $\lambda^2 + 7\pi^2 = 0$ gives roots $\lambda = \pm \sqrt{7}\pi \textrm i.$ So, we have

$$
y_c = A\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $y_p(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition $y'(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
y'(x) \sim B(\sqrt{7}\pi)\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n\pi^2\left(28-n^2\right)} \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
$$

Applying $y'(0)=0$ and noting that $\cos(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B(\sqrt{7}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\ B(\sqrt{7}\pi ) & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{7}n{\pi }^{3}(28-{n}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into $y_c = B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)\sim 
\bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{-\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^n}{\sqrt{7}n\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)}}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231568 :question/id #uuid "77e4924e-4e5a-5efe-907f-1d410dafb965" :question/math-academy-id "q-343467" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231419 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81f5380b-7a7d-52c5-a530-3768e7cf3143" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Second-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ce2f1c7b-a4fc-5268-91ca-e63ea6ba485f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sin (\sqrt{5}x)(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} + ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)\frac{nb_{n}}{\sqrt{5}})" :db/id 17592186230286} {:answer/id #uuid "d98cb78c-8304-501e-8b76-145d03bc45dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\cos (\sqrt{5}x)(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} - ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)\frac{nb_{n}}{\sqrt{5}})" :db/id 17592186230287} {:answer/id #uuid "149cfff1-6f68-5b1c-816b-22b353455f0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sin (\sqrt{5}x)(4 - ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)nb_{n})" :db/id 17592186230288} {:answer/id #uuid "3c3a4ebb-2118-5a42-b1e7-432cc4416187" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sin (\sqrt{5}x)(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} - ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)\frac{nb_{n}}{\sqrt{5}})" :db/id 17592186230289}] :answer-field/id #uuid "fd04368a-dac0-5433-8c72-d4cb4522f0aa" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494 :db/ident :answer-field.type/select} :db/id 17592186230285}] :question/problem "$y^{″} + 5y = f(x), y(0) = 0, y^{′}(0) = 4$

:answer-field.type/select} :db/id 17592186365949}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-5
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =B\sqrt{3}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{3} & =-5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365954 :question/id #uuid "fdb89387-1831-5dc9-8b54-30b782e40107" :question/math-academy-id "q-343989"} {:db/id 17592186365960 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231810 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231984 :tutorial/content "We know how to find a Fourier-series particular solution $y_p$ for a periodically forced linear ODE. In this topic, the new step is how to use $y_p$ to satisfy an initial condition.

Recall that once a particular solution $y_p$ is chosen, the full solution has the form $$y = y_c + y_p,$$ where $y_c$ solves the corresponding homogeneous equation.

Now, suppose the IVP is given at $x=x_0{:}$ $$y(x_0)=y_0.$$ Then, $$y_0 = y_c(x_0)+y_p(x_0).$$

A useful simplification is to choose the particular solution so that $$y_p(x_0)=0.$$ In that case, the initial condition becomes $$y_0 = y_c(x_0),$$ so we can solve for the constant(s) in $y_c$ immediately (without evaluating any Fourier sums at $x_0$).

On the next slide, we’ll apply this idea in an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4a6bfce3-0ee4-5ea7-905f-461e3f15500e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14713 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1d2d573d-acda-5605-a740-470ab9c3110a" :step/math-academy-id 607581 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231811}} {:db/id 17592186231811 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231993 :tutorial/content "For example, consider the initial value problem $$y'-2y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,$$ where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Suppose we choose the forcing (and hence the Fourier-series particular solution) so that $$y_p(0)=0.$$

First, solve the homogeneous equation: $$y' - 2y = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_c = Ae^{2x}.$$

A $2$-periodic forcing function can be written using harmonics of frequency $\pi$, so we may write the particular solution in the form $$y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).$$ Thus the full solution is $$y(x)=Ae^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).$$

Now apply $y(0)=3$ and use $y_p(0)=0$: $$\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{2(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 3 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}$$

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form $$y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)$$ with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:

- **Case 1:** $f(x)$ is odd.

If $f(x)$ is *odd* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *odd*, so it is a sine series: $$y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)$$ This immediately gives $y_p(0)=0,$ so the condition $y(0)=y_0$ determines the cosine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.
- **Case 2:** $f(x)$ is even.

If $f(x)$ is *even* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *even*, so it is a cosine series: $$y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)$$ Here, the derivative is a sine series: $$y_p'(x)=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{a_n n\pi}{L} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)$$ This immediately gives $y_p'(0)=0,$ so the condition $y'(0)=y_1$ determines the sine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.

In both cases, the key idea is that evaluating at $x=0$ (and differentiating once) lets the initial conditions pick off the constants in $y_c$ as cleanly as possible.

Let's see how this works in practice on the next slide." :tutorial/id #uuid "c8c0ab68-168a-57f1-9ab6-13bd9d042d32" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14781 :tutorial/title "Second-Order IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "ffe83dea-ed44-5451-a483-e07ad7977f77" :step/math-academy-id 607586 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231814}} {:db/id 17592186231814 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231990 :tutorial/content "Consider the initial value problem $$y''+ 7y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,\quad y'(0)=0$$ where $f(x)$ is an even, $2\pi$-periodic function. Since the forcing is even and the differential operator contains no $y'$ term, we represent the particular solution as a cosine series: $$y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx)$$

Next, we solve the homogeneous equation $y''+7y=0.$ The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2+7=0,$ so $$y_c=A\cos(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{7}x).$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives $$y'(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\sin(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\cos(\sqrt{7}x)-\sum_{n=1}^\infty n a_n\sin(nx).$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}},$ where

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives the system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 5 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=2 \\ 5{x}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+2(2)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2.
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=(-2)+2=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186120380 :question/id #uuid "c84ba5cc-de62-58a0-bc75-0d770193bc68" :question/math-academy-id "q-35233"} {:db/id 17592186247252 :question/id #uuid $$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives the system with the augmented matrix 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 6 \\ 5 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 6 \\ 5 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 22 & 22 \\ 0 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{22}{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 22 & 22 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=6 \\ 22{x}_{2}=22.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+4(1)=6\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2.
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
